newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Shun Tak seen suffering from Macau crime.
newsitem.headline: HK's Shun Tak seen suffering from Macau crime.

text.p: Hong Kong-listed jetfoil operator and hotel owner Shun Tak Holdings Ltd may see a small upturn in earnings this year despite a crime wave in neighbouring Macau which analysts say is hurting tourism.
"What's happening there is definitely not good for tourism," Fred Kam, senior investment analyst at New China Hong Kong, said on Tuesday.
On Sunday, three men were shot dead in broad daylight in a car on Avenida de Praia Grande, one of the Portuguese-run enclave's main streets.
The killings brought Macau's murder rate this year to 14 against 21 in all of 1996. Police have linked the slayings to warfare among triads, or organised criminal gangs.

Shun Tak runs regular jetfoil service between Hong Kong and Macau, 60 km to the west, and holds stakes in three of the enclave's top hotels. Macau is a popular getaway for Hong Kong people for its casinos and restaurants.

Shun Tak shares ended Tuesday morning's session up HK$0.025 at HK$4.90 on thin trade of HK$4.41 million. The Hang Seng Index ended the morning session 181.19 points, or 1.35 percent, higher at 13,580.53.
The company's 1996 results, which were much worse than most analysts had forecast, already showed the impact of the rising crime wave in Macau, analysts said.
In March, the company reported a 41.34 percent fall in 1996 earnings to HK$421.5 million, citing a decline in passenger traffic on its main Hong Kong-Macau route and over-capacity.
But analysts are expecting the company to report a slight rise in earnings in 1997, when compared with the low 1996 base.
"Jetfoil operations will be the main contributor to earnings this year," said Kam.
Fuel prices, one of the company's chief costs, had declined after rising 19.5 percent in 1996.
"It is a bit early to say but it looks like jetfoil fuel prices will be much lower on average this year," said Kam.
Another analyst who follows the company also forecast lower jetfuel costs.
Kam is forecasting earnings of HK$450 million in 1997, a 6.89 percent rise and higher than the consensus forecast of two percent growth.
The company's earnings outlook is also dependent on tourism trends because of its investment in three five-star hotels in Macau.
Shun Tak has a 50 percent stake in the Mandarin Oriental, a 34.9 percent holding in the Westin Resort and an 11.1 percent stake in the Bela Vista.
In 1996, the hotel division is estimated to have contributed pre-tax profits of about HK$24 million, or about five percent of the total.

The company is also affected by tourist traffic through its five percent stake in Sociedade de Turismo e Diversoes de Macau (STDM), a privately-held company that holds the exclusive casino franchise and runs a lottery and race tracks in the enclave.
Gaming mogul Stanley Ho is also group executive chairman of Shun Tak.
Shun Tak's investment income in 1996 was estimated at about HK$100 million before tax, with just about half of that derived from STDM, analysts said.
